Orwell is a game where you investigate a crime (a bombing, to be precise) using the brand-new Orwell system, presumably named after famous author George Orwell, author of 1984. Using the program, you can identify data that might be necessary to your investigation, slowly collecting it and linking it together to form a case for your superior to take a look at and give his verdict.

Some data is useless; do you really need to know what this woman's favourite colour or food is? Is someone's address being "somewhere over the rainbow" on one of their social networking profiles pertinent information to the case? No, and adding too much useless data can cloud the system, leading to the wrong conclusion by your supervisor at the end. One of my personal favourites was having someone logged in on someone else's account mention their profession, and it came up as data for the account's owner. Presumably, if in an online chat, you joked you killed a man, or were a descendant of King Arthur, that would show up in the Orwell system as important information.

Other data is in conflict; for example, if a Facebook timeline would have someone changing their relationship status to "in  a relationship with whoever", and then later changing it to "single", which one would be the correct data to input? You cannot remove data once you upload, so you have to think long and hard about which to use. Of course, in this example, you could look at whichever was more recent, but the decisions can be harder and more complicated than that, I promise you. I commend this game having pieces of in-conflict data show up as conflicted even if you haven't found the other data yet, so you can't choose A (the only option at the time) and then have option B, the secret correct answer, be revealed to you later.

You also have the ability to, once you have contact details (such as phone numbers, email addresses, etc.), access your target's phone calls, emails, chat histories. These play out in real time, but you can easily go back to searching through websites for info, and return once the conversation is done.

And I won't spoil anything, but the ending of the second episode had me almost falling off my seat in anticipation and anxiety, hoping my guesses weren't wrong. I punched the air and shouted "YES" pretty loudly when it was revealed I was correct. The game got me way more emotionally involved than I was expecting.

If the idea of this interests you, buy the game. It'll definitely be worth the money. If you're on the fence, never fear! There is a free demo which contains the first episode of five. You now have no reason not to go try it. Go try it.

Orwell is a classic example of doing wonders using very little. 

It won't blow you away with the graphics, but combined with the immersive, gentle soundtrack that dynamically changes as you play, and a captivating story and well written content, you'll be hooked. 

I've always very much been a fan of slower paced games that involve alot of surrounding story and Orwell provides it in droves, without being a very clumsy political statement by itself. You're dropped into the "Orwell" system and told to go to work investigating a terrorist attack, but there are no clear cut moral choices, you read the information given to you, submit what is pertinent and do your job, all the while slowly being drawn into your role as an investigator - all without a single action sequence or quicktime event. 

If atmospheric games are your thing, give it a go. The interface is clean, intuitive, the soundtrack is hauntingly beautiful, and the whole story will keep you glued to your government workstation for the duration.
The storyline is emensely compelling.

By far the best indie I have played in a while (except This is The Police). 

Literally played this with my 38-year-old copy of George Orwell's -no pun intended- 1984, in order to feel the climate of this game. It's story is intriguing, makes you sit a bit and think what info you should convey and besides it's current small length, it has the potential to keep you interested for hours.

The ending was amazing. I recommend this totally.

I really love the feeling of the game, the story so far and how it unfolds. The art style is nice, too. Also I really love the feeling of distress I got, when deciding  to which person to attribute certain actions. I was really stressed in the end of episode 2, when I decided on the final information.

The feeling of this game is quite immersive eventhough one "only" deals with text. Be warned though, that for the first 2 episodes you will only need around 2-3 hours if you read everything. Until now it was mostly interactive story telling, the good kind, and deciding on some conflicting information. Hopefully the following episodes become even more uncertain. :)

Waiting for episode 3 now.

This is a very hard game to pin down but is kind of like Uplink meets Papers Please with a visual novel style. It really does a great job of defying easy classification and it is brilliant at embracing moral ambiguity. There are a lot of times when there is no clear right answer and you have to go with your gut or personal moral compass rather than playing a clearly good/evil role as a player. I will be very interested to see where the story goes as it is being released in episodes, but so far I think George would be pleased to have this game to his name.

This game has something really intriguing going for it, plus it also has a really nice ascetic touch to it as well.
It's not so much the "spying" part of this game that makes it the most interesting for me, but more so how the real theme of the game is the perception of information. 

How you perceive what you see, and what you choose to upload affects what they get to see and also how they perceive what you give them. Some of the information you can chose to upload can either be red hearings, outright false, and some that have no right answer.

If you're unsure about the game try the free demo while it is still available as the dev has said it won't be around forever, then if you love it as I did go ahead and buy the game, it will be well worth it.

It's 5 minutes into the future, in a fictional nation where you have just joined a secret government organization whose job it is to gather information, sometimes publicly available, sometimes deeply private and personal, and use it to prevent and solve crime.

Your job is to rifle through this information and pass snippets of it that you deem important to the case over to your superiors, who will constantly give you feedback and requests for more. It doesn't take long before you realize that this is a horrible system where your personal opinions and feelings can decide what picture is painted of the people you investigate, and that "Nothing to hide, nothing to fear" is as empty and absurd as saying that only troublemakers need freedom of speech or personal lives. And your superiors are constantly suspicious of everyone.

Facebook posts deleted after the medicated user had an outburst...nothing to hide, nothing to fear.
Take statements out of context and ruin peoples lives with them...nothing to hide, nothing to fear.
Cherrypick contradicting statements and go with the interpretation you feel like. Did the attack happen in defense, or out of anger? Nothing to hide, nothing to fear.
Cause tension in a relationship by reporting the theft of a credit card that one had willingly lent to the other. Nothing to hide, nothing to fear.

Thanks for reading my review, NSA.

Orwell is a unique text-based investigation game related to a novel called 1984 by George Orwell. The game already highlights somewhat important parts of the text. However, it is up to you to upload the information, and your decisions will matter in the future episodes. You will be spying not only on the social posts, but also on the private chats, calls and emails of the suspects. As you move on, you will even be able to access some crucial data on your suspects' PCs.

Graphicwise, the game has got a stunning interface and a great webchunk system.

Although people are complaining about the shortage of the game. It is not that short and I would estimate that every episode is around 45-60 minutes. Anyways, I would prefer better experience rather than a longer and boring one.

To conclude this review, if you have enough enthusiasm to not rush and play the game slowly by reading and understanding most (or all) of the information which requires a decent amount of English knowledge, I recommend you to buy this game.

This game is close to being unique (it's a bit Hacknet/Uplink but with a wonderfully minimal UI and no typing (yet), it also reminds me of a 90s game called Floor 13 which was about conducting political espionage), is interesting and smart, and is just overall fun to play. If you want to embroil yourself in convicting people of crimes based on things they've basically written on Facebook then go for it.

Negatives: The choices, I suspect, will only ever be binary. The fact that the game flags up conflicting data-chunks **even thought you've only seen the first one of the two** works against the immersion slightly.

But overall I'd wholeheartedly recommend this to anyone who wants to play a game about heavy-handed surveillance culture where anything anyone does works against them.

The Good: Amazing world development, excellent sense of tension, powerful story, and genuinely intriguing.  Also, it would have been easy to over-moralize, instead they make their moral point in small ways.  You stop a bombing but accidentally used the fact someone said they'd "torture" a friend jokingly to have them declared a potentially dangerous person.  It comes off as a more intelligent and incisive commentary on the Surveilance State, the NSA, PRISM and the like because it wasn't completely one-sided.  

The Bad:  The intro shows a watch_Dogs style "popup information about people walking by a camera" interface that looks awesome.  This is the only time you will see it.  While the interface as it is has varied info sources using the cameras that keep getting mentioned might be nice!  On the other hand maybe that's a political statement, that you leave enough intel they don't need CCTV everywhere to track you... I don't know.  
It's pretty short, though at this price point I forgive that.

The Ugly:  Episodic construction means you will be waiting on tenterhooks for the next one.

Get this if:  You liked the idea behind Westport Independent, you watch Mr. Robot, If you thought Watch_Dogs and CtOS were a fascinating idea poorly delivered,  If you like cyberpunk in general.

Suggested price point:  Pay full price, you won't regret the ride.

In this game, you play as a special government agent, who's job is to make your country secure from terrorists. 

The game is divided into 5 episodes, there are 2 episodes released as of the time of writing. Each episode is a "day" at work. When investigating, you search through data on the virtual "internet", which is full of interesting things to explore and read, both important to your mission and fillers.

Graphics are simple, clean and very easy to look at.

Sounds are simple, no voice acting present (unfortunately).

Music is ambient, mostly relaxing, when things happen it gets much more energetic, adding to the atmosphere.

Throughout the game you work with your co-worker Symes. He has interesting insight into the problems at hand and is generaly not intrusive - leaving the problem solving to you which is excelent.

The main thing - the Story is very interesting. It is just exciting enough and believeable enough, that you can really dive deep into it. Each character has it's backstory and is written very well.

Overall, I think this game is absolutely worth the EUR 10 price. It's fun, interesting and get's you thinking. They could easily make this into a "season" game, releasing 5-6 episode in a season for 5-10 bucks every now and then.

After playing through the first two episodes, I can't wait for future sory to be released. Looking forward to a mroe detailed review as more episodes are released in coming weeks.

It's so easy to get invested in the lives of little people when you can instantly find info about them on the internet, posts they've made, read their E-Mails, listen in on their phone calls and violate privacy in other ways.

EDIT: I've decided to add some more on to this review, since I really do think this game is good, and it deserves a more detailed review than what I wrote.

There's one thing that I really want people to know about in this game. Other reviews will probably talk about everything else, but what really caught my attention is how well characterized this world they've created is.

The developers did a really good job at presenting not only the people, but also the issues the game touches on firmly and equally. In any other game, or even film or book, it would no doubt be written to make the Government a bunch of faceless, freedom hating cronies who only feel passion from taking away liberties from the people, and to portray the rebels as the uncompromising heroes of humanity and answer to every problem possible. Instead, the developers made both sides of the 'war' have their strengths and weaknesses in every interpretation of the term. For example: the Government you work for is clearly doing good things, and the Orwell program puts you in contact with Symes, a human handler, who is just like any other person in the game: he has a personality and a history in game, is very friendly to the player and is clearly passionate in his work for the Government. My point is, the developers do a really good job at making them seem like they're doing good, and even makes you sympathise with the good the Government is doing, despite some of the questionable things they do in game and the horrific implications of even having a program like Orwell in the works.

Meanwhile, the "rebel" group that you spend each episode investigating is full of young, flawed people who seem more like a disfunctional group of friends than any liable threat to national security. As you investigate each member, you come to understand their personalities and struggles, but (to me at least) never fully support what they're doing or why they are doing it.

This is what earned a recommendation from me.

TL;DR: The games is good because instead of taking the quick and easy path, they make both sides of the 'war' and in extension the argument realistic positives and negatives.

This game could easily keep one absorbed for hours. It doesn't mess about and places you slap bang in the middle of an ever expanding conspiracy, ramping up the tension and forcing you to act. You will be forced to reason and employ sound logic to get through, with each decision you make raising the stakes even further. With no way to reverse the decisions you've made, you better hope you've made the right ones.

Having played this game up to the conclusion of the second chapter, I find myself astounded by how quickly the tension in a game can rise when all you're doing is playing around with text. It really is a game that can get the heart racing at points, and you'll find yourself crossing your fingers and waiting in silent anticipation as you see the results of your actions unfold. A truly thrilling experience, with fantastic scope for expansion in the future and the occasionally subtle Orwell reference thrown in for those familiar with the (loose) source material.

Definitely one I'd recommend.

You love deeply narrative and morally-not-so-obvious games?
Then ORWELL is for you!

Mix Papers, Please; Her Story and George Orwell into one game and here you go.
Orwell is one of the most clever stories I have ever read, put into distopian reality of the Big Brother's Country.
Are you going to spy and violate one's privacy to protect safety of your fellow citizen or avoid it as much as you can and let bad events happen? 
The choice is yours and there is no good answer, nor path.

The most important question is - is it still a fictional game or slowly a real scenario?

The game is really great so far (Episode 1&2). 
Very well polished, great Story, great UI (could use a tad better click/mouseover-detection though).
The game puts you in the shoes of an investigator - reading through other peoples mail, communication etc to find connections to terrorist attacks. 
You often have to rely on your judgement which parts to submit. They sometimes contradict each other and are submitted largely without context - so you could easily put suspicion on a person for a throwaway comment on the internet.
The game really gives you a chilly feeling of "how realistic is this?" - its awesome so far.

This is really immersive game play! 10/10
The visuals are unique. The look of an desktop work environment and the sounds draw me into the world of Orwell.

I just played the beginning of the story, now. But I feel the responsibility and suspicions against the people and the system itself. It's hard to describe ... it is a special game play experience for me!
I got the game and will stay tuned to the further episodes of Orwell: yes, I keep an eye on you!
